report:
**Conclusion: usually no.** For most people, taking vitamin C regularly does **not meaningfully prevent getting colds**. The best evidence—a Cochrane review of 29 randomized trial comparisons (11,306 participants)—found no important reduction in cold incidence in the general population (relative risk 0.97; 95% CI 0.94–1.00). Routine supplementation solely to prevent colds therefore is not supported.

There is an important exception: in people undergoing short periods of **severe physical stress** (for example, marathon runners, skiers, or military personnel in very cold conditions), trials found roughly a halving of cold incidence. That evidence does not establish the same benefit for everyday life.

Regular supplementation may still offer a *small different benefit*: among people who do catch a cold, duration was reduced by about **8% in adults and 14% in children** in the Cochrane analysis. Starting vitamin C only after symptoms begin has not shown consistent benefit.

So, the claim is partly right only for specific high-stress groups—not as a general cold-prevention strategy. Adequate vitamin C intake remains important for health, but higher-dose supplements are not a reliable shield against colds; NIH also notes that most people do not have a lower cold risk from supplements.

Sources:  
- https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold  
- https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23440782/  
- https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminC-Consumer/  
- https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/colds-flu-and-complementary-health-approaches
